<reason>Both sides were excellent, but CON built more surviving routes to victory. PRO's burden-reversal frame (uncertainty defaults to no access vs. defaults to market) was coherent and directly defended in the A1:/A2: answers. But CON repeatedly turned PRO's own premises: the irreversibility that PRO invoked via catastrophic misuse (pathogens, infrastructure) is precisely the channel an EU market-access gate cannot reach — those models never file applications — forcing PRO to retreat to the narrower "lawful deployment scaling" harm. CON also caught PRO's GDPR analogy as a behaviour-based regime with the opposite architecture, and showed the suspension lever is as ex post as a fine under PRO's own proliferation premise. CON's pressure question extracted a "Yes" that surviving use-level duties reduce the motion to risk-based-plus-gate, and CON's closing inverted PRO's best line ("Refuse whose entry?"). PRO's closing reasserted that the status quo is "all ex post" after CON had corrected that with pre-market conformity assessment — an unrebutted mischaracterization. Both sides had one clipped turn, roughly cancelling. PRO was polished and honest in its answers, but CON left the cleaner comparative: the gate binds only the compliant, adds a stamp and a moat, and reaches none of the threats PRO opened with.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1: flipping PRO's GDPR analogy (a conduct-based regime, the opposite architecture from an entry gate) and showing that licence suspension is exactly as reactive as a fine once weights proliferate — "PRO's own premise kills their own remedy." The closing echo ("Refuse whose entry?") sealed it.</best_rebuttal>
